147.t: The segregated Cotton Club and Bill Robinson's way in
147.s: Crawford says the club admitted no Black patrons except Bill Robinson, and entertainers who objected would be fired.
147.ch: New York, the Lafayette and the Cotton Club
147.q: Bill Robertson. Bill Robertson, you know how he got in there. Tam his way in, (Inaudible) you know, that laugh. Somebody like Woogie Harris, who they knew had a lot of money. I don't know whether you know Woogie Harris.

147.t: Waiters' tips, Jack Johnson and Joe Louis at the Cotton Club
147.s: Crawford says waiters got the tips, that Jack Johnson first started the club and he later met him, and that Joe Louis got in with Bill Robinson.
147.ch: New York, the Lafayette and the Cotton Club
147.q: -- all those waiters. Kid Griffith was the head waiter, and all those other guys like that, they'd get nice tips, they got nice tips, waiters. Oh, that was big time. You know how that place first started? Jack Johnson.

147.t: Musicians restricted by the club's policy; Cab Calloway
147.s: Crawford says only big names like Ellington or Calloway might object to the policy, and says he liked Calloway.
147.ch: New York, the Lafayette and the Cotton Club
147.q: Maybe Duke Ellington or Cab Calloway, but they were big boys.

18.s: Mrs. JCH says nightlife was all uptown and downtown had nothing; Armstrong met Lucille at the Cotton Club.
18.ch: Union, publishers, race and Harlem nightlife
18.q: You wouldn't have made it so good. Harlem was the best place for you to live in those days. You couldn't live downtown so good.

18.t: Hanging out at the Copper Rail without discrimination
18.s: Musicians hung out across from the Metropole, white and black together.
18.ch: Union, publishers, race and Harlem nightlife
18.q: No discrimination, everybody just laugh and talk. All musicians meet in there, white and Negros.

97.t: Women instrumentalists; after-hours Harlem rounds of the Rhythm Club and Small's
97.s: Asked about Leora, he describes the mixed orchestras of Harlem and where musicians went after work.
97.q: think? Well, I tell you, in those days, there weren't many colored people in Harlem. And there -- a good deal of white people came there, and you had a mixed orchestra, a couple of white women was in there. And they didn't think anything, everything was all right. We didn't have any crime in those…

97.t: Lindy's and Harlem history: no experience of discrimination
97.s: Scott describes being served at Lindy's and says he experienced no discrimination as a professional.
97.q: And it was good to be back on Broadway again, because I'd been down there with Fletcher and Duke and then there was different places to go around and renew old acquaintenances and like that, because those white fellows that played down that way, you're going to meet them down that way. And they…

251.t: Pictures of his parents and the New York band and nightclub
251.s: His mother and father, then the New York band at age 23 with blue tails and his integrated nightclub.
251.q: Yes, very talented and well raised and she has all good traits about her. Very smart in school, makes all A's and B's. This is my mother that was taken out at Lake Punch and Train one year that I went to visit them. Oh yeah. You recognize that? That's the seawall. That's the seawall. Yeah. My…

151.t: Reuben Hughes and the Baruch family's Club Zombie
151.s: Reason explains Saul Broad as the owner of the nightclub where they played.
151.q: Saul Broad was, as you know, the Jewish guy owned the nightclub where we played called Broad's Club Zombie.

812.t: Piano players, mob-owned clubs and Waldorf audiences
812.s: She recalls clubs like Jilly's, and Waldorf guests including Cunard travelers and tourists asking about Cole Porter.
812.q: Oh yeah. Oh, oh — we piano players observe everything. And we’re ready. You know in the old days when the mob owned a lot of the clubs, which is really something that we miss in this business. Those clubs are gone, like Jilly’s. That’s where I started. Jimmy Weston’s — and all over the country…

369.t: Who ran the Morocco's business, its acts and how long it lasted
369.s: His sisters handled the money; acts included Wild Bill Davis; it opened in 1953 and lasted a year.
369.ch: School, women pianists and the Chicago style
369.q: He didn’t want me to handle none of the money. He had his sisters handle it. Everything he had, he had in his peoples’ name. If he moved to a woman’s house, he’d only take his toothbrush.

135.t: Monte Kay, Birdland and the mob-run New York clubs
135.s: Heath recalls meeting Monte Kay in 1952, the Levys' ownership of Birdland, and the double standard that kept Monk without a cabaret card.
135.q: He was involved with Birdland and he pulled out from Birdland, Morris Levy and his brother, Irving, and some other, hooked up, connected Jewish owners. All those clubs in New York at that time were run by the so-called mob, and Morris Levy was connected, otherwise they wouldn’t be in business. But…

704.t: Naomi Campbell, Hugo Chavez, Castro at Birdland and the Theresa Hotel
704.s: Jones talks about Naomi Campbell as a daughter, a call from Hugo Chavez, meeting Castro at Birdland after the revolution, the Theresa Hotel, Ron Brown and Malcolm X.
704.q: It’s awesome. It’s funny, because Naomi Campbell’s like my daughter, 16 years. Mandela’s her grandpoppy. I’m poppy. She’s the sweetest girl in the world, but boy, she can do it. She’s always into something. “Poppy” – she’s a writer now, one of the editorial staff for GQ. “Poppy.” “Yes baby?”…

64.t: Minton's clientele, women audiences and mixed crowds in Harlem
64.s: He describes the hustlers and fast life around Minton's, the safe atmosphere for unescorted women, and downtown audiences and clubs like the Twenty-One that excluded Black people.
64.ch: Arriving in New York and 52nd Street
64.q: Minton’s was a place where a lot of pimps, and hustlers, and people who lived the fast life partied. They met there. They hung around the bar in the daytime and played the numbers and bet on the horses and so forth. Henry Minton was a former delegate to the musicians union and he bought the place.…

26.s: Greer says prices kept most Black patrons away; Bill Robinson was welcome.
26.q: We were so busy -- we didn't pay it no mind. Because in the first place, we had colored people come up there, but the prices were so high. The average colored person back off. They could go to Small's Paradise and them clubs, and that -- when you come in the Cotton Club, you sit down, you're going…

9.t: Cotton Club celebrity nights and who could get in
9.s: The Cotton Club had a Black show and band but a White clientele, with Sunday celebrity nights, and Black patrons could get in if they could pay.
9.q: : Oh yeah. The Cotton Club at that time, they entertained nothing but Hollywood celebrities. Sunday night was their Celebrity Night at the Cotton Club, and anybody who was ever a star in Hollywood, as soon as they'd come to New York, they would be at the Cotton Club that Sunday night.

70.t: White patronage of Harlem, after-hours joints and copied riffs
70.s: In the early thirties whites flocked safely to Harlem clubs and after-hours spots, and downtown musicians wrote down riffs on their cuffs.
70.ch: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
70.q: Oh, definitely. And, you know, a lot of them used to come up to Harlem back in the early thirties, you know, when a lot of white musicians and white people used to come up to Harlem to hang out. There was no muggings. Nobody bothered anybody in those days. And Harlem was a beautiful place. A lot of…

91.t: Harlem clubs for black audiences versus white-only places
91.s: He distinguishes Harlem clubs welcoming black patrons from Connie's Inn and the Cotton Club, and after-hours spots like Mexico's.
91.ch: Harlem scene and race in music
91.q: Which is where the musicians even like, musicians when they got through playing down at the Roseland with Fletcher Henderson and playing the arrangements, they would come up to places like the Rhythm Club or some of the late hour places that were big. Mexico's, a place called Mexico's on 133rd…

235.t: Who owned and managed the Paradise
235.s: New Orleans manager Bill Jameison, owners from cigarette vending and general manager Hilda ran the 110th Street club.
235.ch: The Paradise and life in Queens
235.q: Well, it was people that um...Bill Jameison managed it. He was from New Orleans; he was the manager and he loved music. So that was in our favor. Whatever we did he was all for it. 'Cause most of these New Orleans people, they love music. And he was a New Orleans man'. And I'll never

168.t: Cafe Society opening in 1938 as the first integrated New York club
168.s: Stewart was about to leave for the Coast in 1938; Crouch relays Barney Josephson's account that other clubs admitted Black musicians but not Black patrons.
168.ch: Rose Murphy, wartime 52nd Street, Town Hall
168.q: Well, I didn't notice that. I wasn't out in the, what I mean, myself personally, I wasn't around when I would hear a statement on that order where the club was an integrated (inaudible).

6.t: Playing and visiting the Cotton Club
6.s: He filled in with a house band at the Cotton Club a few times and visited with Duke and Cab; he is unsure whether Black customers were allowed but walked in.
6.ch: Early records, Detroit and Prohibition-era nightlife
6.q: No. No. Well, yeah, I played in there a few times with just a fill-in band, you know, somebody to play up there awhile, to be the house band, that was off somewhere.

75.t: 125th Street, Duke Yelman and the Cotton Club color line
75.s: He describes 125th Street as a mosaic, a quarter-a-head club-date band as a substitute for the Cotton Club, and the Cotton Club's exclusion of Black patrons.
75.ch: Early 1930s: Bessie Smith, Rex Stewart and the Harlem scene
75.q: : Yeah. And colors. Ethnic... It was predominantly... I mean, Jewish-owned, but then predominantly the buyers were Blacks and Spanish and things like that. But there was a Duke Yelman(?)... See, if you couldn't go to the Cotton Club to hear Duke Ellington, you paid a quarter and went down and heard…

81.t: The Mob at the Cotton Club and identifying with Black people
81.s: The Cotton Club belonged to the mob and was segregated; Johnson could have passed but wanted to pull others along; he recalls Fats saying 'talk to me, baby'.
81.q: J. C. was pretty reticent about talking about the Mob on tape. But one of the comments that he did make was that the Cotton Club belonged to the Mob and they had it pretty well segregated. He wrote shows for Texas Guynan and in the last two shows Texas Guynan, he mentioned, was ruled by the Mob.

77.t: Dreamland versus New York clubs and the Cotton Club
77.s: Dreamland outclassed New York clubs except perhaps the Cotton Club, which seated Black patrons in the back; Lena Horne's mother was in her first Broadway show with Hunter.
77.q: Oh, Lord, yes. These clubs in New York haven't got a chance with what the Dreamland was. Only the Cotton Club. And the Cotton Club was more -- no, it didn't compare with Dreamland.
